title: Social friendship
hook: friendship across divides, and deep caution about war

segments.voice: Yesterday, Fratelli Tutti and the road to Jericho. Your line was all brothers and sisters. Who did you stop for, and what did those few minutes hold? Day one thousand three hundred seventeen.

Every election season, opposite yard signs go up on two neighboring lawns, and every season the two neighbors stop waving. They used to borrow each other's ladders. Now they check the street before stepping outside so they won't have to talk. Nothing violent has happened. Nobody has done anything wrong, exactly. But something between them has been switched off. Fratelli Tutti, the letter we opened yesterday, has a name for what was lost, and it's the second half of the letter's own subtitle: on fraternity and social friendship. Today is that phrase, and where Francis follows it, all the way to the hardest place, war.
screen: `OPPOSITE YARD SIGNS.` → `SOMETHING SWITCHED OFF.` → `FRATERNITY AND SOCIAL FRIENDSHIP.`

segments.voice: First, what it means. Friendship is usually private: the few people you choose. Social friendship, for Francis, is the same warmth stretched across a whole society. Not agreeing with everyone. Not even liking everyone. But refusing to treat anyone as an enemy by default, and staying at the table. Second, how it's built. Francis puts dialogue at the center: approaching, listening, looking at each other, trying to understand, finding common ground. He warns against the opposite, the feverish exchange of opinions online, where people talk past each other and only hear their own side. Real dialogue, he says, is slow, and it costs something. Third, the hard edge: war. Here Francis is blunt. The Catechism keeps the Church's long teaching that a nation may defend itself under strict conditions, the teaching called just war. Francis doesn't erase it, but he says that with today's weapons it's very hard to meet those old criteria, and he cries out: never again war. Some Catholics read this as a turn toward nonviolence; others read it as a warning within the old teaching. Both look to the same Gospel. Jesus says, in the Douay-Rheims: "Blessed are the peacemakers: for they shall be called the children of God." And on the night he's arrested, when a disciple draws a sword, Jesus says: "Put up again thy sword into its place." Fourth, the link. Put side by side, war looks like social friendship failing at the largest scale. Peace between nations starts small, with two neighbors and a ladder.
screen: `FRIENDSHIP STRETCHED ACROSS A SOCIETY.` · `BUILT BY SLOW, REAL DIALOGUE.` · `DEEP CAUTION ABOUT WAR.` · `PEACE STARTS SMALL.` · then, large: `BLESSED ARE THE PEACEMAKERS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find one person across a divide. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone you've drifted from because of a difference: politics, faith, family history, a side taken in an argument. Don't rehearse the argument. Instead, remember one thing about them you genuinely respect, or one thing you once shared. Then think of one small, low-stakes step toward them: a question about their kids, a recipe, a game you both follow. If you pray, you can hold them before God. If you don't, simply wish them well. The bell holds the time.
Social friendship. Fratelli Tutti's name for friendship stretched across a whole society, built by dialogue, and the opposite of war. Today's word.
Your line: social friendship. Today, take the small step you chose toward someone across a divide, and leave the argument out of it. Day one thousand three hundred seventeen.

howItsDone: Catholics take up Fratelli Tutti's call to social friendship through parish dialogue groups, interfaith and community gatherings, and peace work; Catholic teaching on war is set out in the Catechism, and Francis's caution about it is discussed alongside that teaching.
